archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A pocket-capable thrower who wins by pushing the ball 10-plus yards downfield and turns broken plays into first downs with his legs. Designed runs are not his game.

report.headline: A slow, turnover-heavy September has given way to his 2025 form
report.take:
Maye's 2025 season ranked third in EPA per play, third in CPOE and third in yards per attempt. The first three weeks of 2026 made that look distant. He finished below zero in passing EPA against Seattle, Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, threw interceptions in bunches, and the season lines still carry that weight: 3.7% interception rate (39th of 45) and 0.192 EPA per dropback (12th). Those are good-not-great numbers, and they misdescribe the player of the last month. Over Weeks 5-7 he has posted 0.526 EPA per dropback, a 12.0 CPOE, a 9.3% TD rate and a 1.0% interception rate. That is a better version of last year, not a fluke against soft defenses. Chicago and the Jets sit mid-pack in defensive EPA.

The engine is the downfield game. On throws of 10+ air yards he is at 0.497 EPA per attempt with a 10.1 CPOE, and his 20+ yard throws produce 0.77 EPA with five touchdowns on 29 attempts. That is where most of his passing value lives. The other piece is his legs. His 23 scrambles average 0.842 EPA and have moved the chains 14 times, and they are why his 211 rushing yards rank fifth at the position despite a designed-run game that has gone nowhere. The pocket work has also quietly improved. His pressure-to-sack rate is 22% (10th of 38), well below the 40.5% of his rookie year and the 35.6% of 2025, even though he is under pressure on 26% of dropbacks (30th).

The averages also hide where the drag comes from, and much of it is not him. Throws behind the line of scrimmage have cost -17.1 EPA on 38 attempts, and his under-center dropbacks run at -0.361 per play. That is an offense whose run game ranks 28th in EPA, so play-action and screens are not getting the help they need. Among his top targets, Hunter Henry, DeMario Douglas and Romeo Doubs are all well above 0.4 EPA per target. A.J. Brown sits at -0.23 on 20 targets, so his throws to Brown have been working against him. The completion percentage is down 6.1 points from 2025, but his bad-throw rate is also down, from 13.2% to 11.2%. That suggests the dip comes more from early-season results and the screen game than from worse ball placement.

Where it heads: the interception rate should keep falling toward his career norm, and the downfield efficiency has held across two seasons, so it looks real. The open question is protection. A starting guard is on IR and the center is out, and his red-zone and late-and-close numbers (both slightly negative EPA, three interceptions in each) are small samples but worth tracking.

strengths.title: Downfield accuracy drives the offense
strengths.body: His value is concentrated on throws of 10+ air yards, where he completes well above expectation and has added the bulk of his passing EPA. It is not a one-year spike: his aDOT and aggressiveness rose in 2025 alongside top-3 efficiency, and the deep numbers this year are in line with that. The deep catch rate will always be modest, but the payoff per attempt is large enough to carry an offense with no run game.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move the chains
strengths.body: When plays break down he leaves the pocket with purpose. His scrambles produce 0.842 EPA apiece and have moved the chains 14 times, while his designed runs have been stuffed. This has been consistent: he ranked 9th and 4th in QB rushing yards in his first two seasons. It also explains the long time to throw. He is holding the ball to create, and the improved pressure-to-sack rate shows it is not costing him sacks.

strengths.title: Back to 2025 level lately
strengths.body: Over his last three games his efficiency is above his career-best season. He has a 12.0 CPOE, 10.79 adjusted net yards per dropback and one interception on 97 attempts. Some of the 0.526 EPA per dropback will cool, but the stretch matches the player he showed for a full 17 games last year, so the September version looks like the outlier.

concerns.title: Turnovers, mostly front-loaded
concerns.body: Eight interceptions in seven games already equals his 2025 total, and he has lost two fumbles with five turnover-worthy fumbles overall. Most of the interception damage came in the first three weeks, including three against Seattle's second-ranked defense. The rate has dropped sharply since. It is partly the price of an aggressive downfield style, but ball security in the pocket is a real habit to watch.

concerns.title: Screens and under-center snaps lose value
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have been a steady loss, and under-center dropbacks are deeply negative. Both point to an offense whose 28th-ranked run game gives play-action no punch and whose screen game is not blocking well. That is a scheme and personnel problem rather than a Maye flaw. Still, it caps his floor on weeks when the downfield shots aren't there.

concerns.title: Protection thinning up front
concerns.body: He is already pressured at one of the higher rates among qualifiers. Now starting guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (89% of snaps) is on IR until late November, and center Ben Brown is out for Week 8. His sack avoidance has held up, but more free rushers would test the extended-play style, and his red-zone and late-and-close numbers already sag on small samples.

trend.note: Negative passing EPA in each of Weeks 1-3, then double-digit passing EPA in all four games since. That run includes a 29.5 against Las Vegas and a 15.3 CPOE at Chicago on a short week.

nextGame.headline: League's worst pass defense, with almost no pass rush
nextGame.body:
Miami ranks 32nd in EPA allowed per dropback and 32nd in success rate allowed. It sacks quarterbacks at the second-lowest rate in the league and ranks 30th against deep throws. That lines up almost perfectly with what Maye does: hold the ball, push it 10-plus yards and punish coverage busts. The one cold spot is the opposing WR1, whom Miami has held well under his average. That matters little here, since his production runs through Henry, Douglas and Doubs rather than A.J. Brown. Miami has been gashed by tight ends, which points straight at Henry. It also allows quarterbacks 2.5 touchdowns a game (27th).

Availability cuts both ways. New England is without center Ben Brown and guard Vera-Tucker, so the interior is patched, but this pass rush is among the least threatening he will see. Tackle Marcus Bryant practiced fully and may be close. Miami is down linebacker Willie Gay Jr. (52% of snaps) and edge Robert Beal Jr., which further thins a weak front and its middle-of-the-field coverage. The Patriots are 7.5-point road favorites with 10 days of rest. The main risk to his volume is a lopsided score against a run-heavy, 26th-ranked Miami offense.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a broken secondary
keyMatchups.body: Miami allows over a full point of EPA on deep throws, among the worst marks in the league. Maye's 20+ yard throws are his most valuable plays. With little pressure to speed him up, this is where a big day comes from.

keyMatchups.title: Hunter Henry vs the linebackers
keyMatchups.body: Miami ranks last in EPA allowed to opposing top tight ends, and Gay's absence weakens the coverage underneath. Henry already leads his receivers in EPA added, so the middle of the field should be open.

keyMatchups.title: Game script against a run-first opponent
keyMatchups.body: Miami runs well below expectation in neutral situations and has a bottom-tier offense. If New England builds a lead, the second half may lean on the run. That would cap attempts more than efficiency, since his numbers when leading by 9+ are positive but modest.

nextGame.watch: Whether the patched interior line, without Ben Brown and Vera-Tucker, gives him clean pockets against a rush that rarely gets home. If it does, the deep game should be there all day.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the second half of the season to look much more like Weeks 4-7 than Weeks 1-3. The downfield efficiency and scramble value have held across two seasons, so they look like who he is. The interception rate should settle well below its current mark, closer to last year's pace. The last-three-game rates (0.526 EPA per dropback, a 9.3% TD rate) will cool, because nobody sustains that. A realistic band is roughly 250-295 passing yards and around two touchdowns a game, plus 20-35 rushing yards from scrambles.

The ceiling depends on the line and the run game. A healthy interior and any improvement on the ground would rescue the screen and play-action game that has cost him all year. A longer injury list would bring more pressure on a player who already sees plenty. Brown turning his targets into positive plays would be pure upside, since the offense has produced at a top-5 passing EPA level without that.
swingFactors: Interior O-line health (Vera-Tucker IR, Ben Brown)
Whether the run game lifts screens and play-action
A.J. Brown becoming a positive target

confidence.note: Seven games split between a poor start and a strong finish. The 2025 track record supports the recent form, but offensive-line injuries add uncertainty.
